cases.title: RCA's Taoyuan Electronics Plant and Its Workers' Cancers
cases.place: Taoyuan, Taiwan
cases.point: Former RCA plant area in Taoyuan (EJAtlas coordinates, approximate)

lenders.name: Radio Corporation of America (RCA), later General Electric and Thomson Consumer Electronics (United States/France) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: RCA ran factories in Taoyuan, Hsinchu and Yilan from 1970 to 1992 through a Taiwanese subsidiary. GE absorbed RCA in 1986 and sold its consumer electronics arm to Thomson Consumer Electronics, the US arm of the French firm Technicolor (Taipei Times; New Bloom).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The plant was a wholly foreign-owned factory making television and other electronic parts (Taipei Times; EJAtlas).

companies.name: Radio Corporation of America (RCA)
companies.role: Owner and operator of the Taoyuan plant, 1970-1992

companies.name: General Electric
companies.role: Owner of RCA from 1986; held liable by Taiwan's courts

companies.name: Thomson Consumer Electronics / Technicolor
companies.role: Bought RCA's consumer electronics arm (1988 per the Taipei Times); held liable by Taiwan's courts

cases.community: The plant used up to 31 organic solvents, including trichloroethylene and tetrachloroethene (Taipei Times). The company dumped toxic waste at the Taoyuan factory, polluting soil and groundwater, and workers living in the factory dormitories drank and washed with untreated water pumped from the same ground (EJAtlas). In the first class action, 237 of 529 workers developed cancer or related illnesses and 78 had died (New Bloom). The RCA Self-Help Association says more than 1,300 people were diagnosed with cancers, and former employees say more than 200 have died (Taipei Times). After contamination was reported in 1991, RCA sold the building and land in 1992 for about NT$1.9 billion (Taipei Times).
cases.ecosystem: Soil and groundwater under the plant were contaminated with chlorinated solvents. Taiwan's Environmental Protection Administration designated the site a permanently polluted zone in 1998, the first such case in the country (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: Deaths are from illness, not violence, and are not counted here. New Bloom reports 78 deaths among the 529 workers in the first case; former workers say more than 200 have died (Taipei Times).
cases.outcome: The workers' association began protesting in 1998 and sued in 2004. In October 2017 the Taiwan High Court ordered NT$718.4 million and added GE to the liable companies (New Bloom). On 16 August 2018 Taiwan's Supreme Court upheld the liability of RCA, GE, Thomson and Technicolor and awarded 262 former workers and relatives about NT$500 million (Eye on Taiwan; the Taipei Times gives NT$564.45 million), sending the emotional-distress part back to the High Court. Judges found RCA had moved assets out of Taiwan, with executives sending US$150 million to overseas accounts, to reduce its liability (Taipei Times). In a second suit the Taipei District Court in December 2019 ordered RCA and its affiliates to pay NT$2.3 billion to 1,120 former employees and family members, subject to appeal (Taipei Times).

sources.title: RCA court ruling a victory for workers, but what now?
RCA ordered to pay NT$2.3bn to ex-workers
Supreme Court awards NT$500 million to 262 former RCA workers
Radio Corporation of America, Taiwan

cases.confidence_note: Taiwan is a high-income economy; the case is kept because foreign ownership (an American company's Taiwanese subsidiary, later held by GE and France's Thomson/Technicolor) and the court awards are confirmed by New Bloom, the Taipei Times and CNA (Eye on Taiwan). Sources give different dates for the sale to Thomson (Taipei Times: 1988; Eye on Taiwan: 1998) and different amounts for the 2018 award. Death and cancer totals beyond the first court case come from the workers. The 2019 ruling could still be appealed.

lvwhy.project: A US-owned electronics plant dumped solvents that contaminated workers' water; Taiwan's courts held RCA and its successors liable.

cases.title: Nandigram Chemical Hub for the Salim Group and the 2007 Police Firing
cases.place: Nandigram, Purba Medinipur, West Bengal, India
cases.point: Nandigram town, Nandigram-I block

lenders.name: Salim Group (Indonesia), through New Kolkata International Development (foreign investor)
lenders.role: The West Bengal government chose the Indonesian Salim Group to build a chemical hub in a special economic zone at Nandigram that needed about 4,000 hectares of farmland (Wikipedia; Millennium Post).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The chemical hub was to be a 50-50 joint venture between New Kolkata International Development, promoted by the Salim Group, and the West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation (Down to Earth, via EJAtlas).

companies.name: Salim Group
companies.role: Chosen investor for the Nandigram chemical hub

cases.community: The state planned a chemical hub for the Salim Group on about 10,000 acres (4,000 ha) of farmland; farmers opposed it and blocked roads into the area from January to March 2007 (Wikipedia; Millennium Post). On 14 March 2007 an operation by more than 3,000 police was launched to break the protesters' control of Nandigram; about 5,000 villagers gathered at the entrances, and police fired, killing 14 and injuring 70 (Wikipedia; Millennium Post). More than 100 people were declared missing (Wikipedia). Business Standard reported that those killed were among villagers refusing to give up their land for the project.
cases.suppression: Police firing on 14 March 2007 killed 14 and injured 70 (Millennium Post; Business Standard). Millennium Post also reports that police and CPI(M) cadres looted and burned houses. The Calcutta High Court declared the firing 'unconstitutional' and without basis in law, ordered the CBI to continue its investigation, and in November 2007 ordered Rs 5 lakh for each family of the dead and Rs 2 lakh for the injured (Business Standard; Millennium Post). In 2017 the CBI charge-sheeted three police officers, including two senior IPS officers, and nine others (Millennium Post).
cases.killed_note: Not counted: 14 villagers were killed by West Bengal police on 14 March 2007 (Business Standard; Millennium Post; Wikipedia). The sources describe the operation as one to break the protesters' control of the area, and Wikipedia reports that the government had announced the project's cancellation in early March, before the firing; no source opened says the police were clearing land for the Salim Group's hub. The Trinamool Congress put the toll at 50; a state minister said 50 people were taken to hospital (Wikipedia).
cases.outcome: The SEZ was shelved, and on 3 September 2007 the chief minister proposed Nayachar island, 30 km from Haldia, for the hub instead (Wikipedia). In November 2007 the High Court ordered compensation for the dead and injured (Business Standard). The CBI later cleared the state government of responsibility for the shooting (Wikipedia), while charging individual officers (Millennium Post). The Left Front lost power in West Bengal in 2011 (Wikipedia).

sources.title: Nandigram violence
High Court orders monetary relief for Nandigram victims
Nandigram carnage: CBI files charge-sheet against 2 IPS officers
Nandigram Chemical Hub, India

cases.confidence_note: Contested on the link: the Salim Group was the named investor for the hub, but no land was taken for it and no source opened ties the 14 March police operation to clearing land for the company; the operation was aimed at retaking an area protesters had held for months, and Wikipedia says the project had been called off in early March. The 14 deaths are therefore recorded but not counted.

lvwhy.land: The state tried to acquire about 4,000 ha of farmland for an Indonesian group's chemical hub; police later fired on villagers who had resisted the acquisition.

cases.title: Rempang Eco-City, Xinyi's Glass Factory Plan and the 2023 Crackdown
cases.place: Rempang Island, Batam, Riau Islands, Indonesia
cases.point: Rempang Island (centre, approximate)

lenders.name: Xinyi Glass (China/Hong Kong) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Reported in 2023 to have pledged about $11.6 billion for a glass and solar panel factory at the centre of the Rempang Eco-City, after President Widodo's July 2023 visit to China (Al Jazeera; EJAtlas). In February 2025 Xinyi said it had reached no agreements or contracts for the project (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The project is a joint venture of the Batam free zone authority (BP Batam) and PT Makmur Elok Graha, working with Xinyi, and was listed as a national strategic project in 2023 (Al Jazeera; EJAtlas).
cases.community: The government announced that Rempang's 7,500 residents would be moved about 60 km from their coastal homes; residents told Al Jazeera they learned only in early September 2023 that they had to leave by the end of the month (Al Jazeera). Four villages faced immediate eviction (EJAtlas), and about 700 families were to be moved in the first stage (Malaysia Now). Police tear gas fired near two schools sent pupils and teachers fleeing into the jungle; a pupil said classmates fainted, and a teacher needed oxygen at a clinic (Al Jazeera).
cases.suppression: On 7 September 2023 security forces used tear gas and water cannon on residents blocking land measurement, and on 11 September police again fired tear gas at a protest of about 1,000 people outside the BP Batam office in Batam and arrested 43 for rioting and resisting officers (EJAtlas; Al Jazeera; Malaysia Now). Mongabay, summarised by the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre in October 2024, reported that company security personnel injured villagers, including a 66-year-old woman whose wrist was broken, and that residents still faced intimidation.
cases.outcome: President Widodo said each resident would get land and a house and that the plan had been poorly communicated (Malaysia Now). The coordinating security minister said security forces should have communicated more clearly (Al Jazeera). In a response dated 3 February 2025, Xinyi Glass said it had not reached any agreements or contracts for the project, had not initiated an eco-city, and had only received preliminary pricing and conditions from Batam authorities (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre).

sources.title: Protests in Indonesia as thousands face eviction for Rempang 'Eco-City'
Indonesia police arrest 43 after riot over industrial park
Indonesia: Locals subjected to violence resulting to injuries, arrests after raising concerns against land development project
Xinyi Glass denies involvement in Rempang Island eco-city project
sources.publisher: Business & Human Rights Resource Centre (company response)

sources.title: Rempang Eco-City Project and solar panel factory, Indonesia

cases.confidence_note: The outside link is disputed: the Xinyi pledge was announced by Indonesian officials and reported by the press, but Xinyi says it signed no agreement or contract and did not initiate the eco-city. The eviction orders, tear gas and arrests are documented; how many families have actually moved is not given in the sources.

lvwhy.land: Islanders were ordered off their land for a factory zone announced around a Chinese glass maker's pledge; police tear gas and 43 arrests followed.

cases.title: Okomu Oil Palm (Socfin) Expansion into Edo Forest Reserves
cases.place: Okomu Forest Reserve and nearby reserves, Ovia South-West and Ovia North-East, Edo State, Nigeria
cases.point: Okomu plantation area (EJAtlas coordinates, approximate)

lenders.name: Socfin (Luxembourg/Belgium) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Majority owner of Okomu Oil Palm Company, bought after the federal government sold the state firm in the 1990s privatization wave (Mongabay).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. Okomu holds a 33,112-hectare concession in Edo State (Mongabay).
cases.community: In 2010 residents of Coconut Camp received a notice to dismantle settlements and crops on nearby land to make way for plantation expansion (Mongabay). Residents of Orhua described losing the farmland they depend on, and women said company guards seized their fishing nets (Mongabay). A researcher from Environmental Rights Action said villagers reported food becoming scarcer after losing farmland, and beatings and intimidation by security forces (Mongabay). Environmental Rights Action (Friends of the Earth Nigeria) alleged that over 11,000 hectares of forest and farmland in the Owan and Ehor forest reserves had been taken (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: Most of the concession lies inside the Okomu Forest Reserve, gazetted in 1912; the group reported bulldozing of the Owan Forest Reserve for expansion (Mongabay; EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: On 1 January 2011 traditional chief Ajele Sunday, a critic, was arrested and accused of planting a bomb at company headquarters; the case was soon dropped. In the following weeks, at Okomu's instruction, soldiers guarding the plantation closed the only road through it from sundown to sunrise; the managing director wrote that the road would stay closed until the community signed a memorandum recognising the company's right to clear the land (Mongabay). A 2020 post by Ajele Sunday accused soldiers and security working with Okomu of torching a small village; the company called it a 'defamatory diatribe' (Mongabay).
cases.killed_note: Five company staff were killed by aggrieved residents in 2015 (Mongabay); not counted, as they were not killed by the company or forces acting for it.
cases.outcome: Okomu's main estate was certified by the RSPO in early 2020; Friends of the Earth Netherlands filed a complaint about the audit with Assurance Services International (Mongabay). Okomu denies taking customary land and says soldiers were deployed on the governor's orders against illegal logging and pipeline sabotage (Mongabay).

sources.title: At a 'certified' palm oil plantation in Nigeria, soldiers and conflict over land
Okomu oil palm plantation, Edo State, Nigeria

cases.confidence_note: The land and road-closure accounts come from Mongabay's reporting. A figure of over 60,000 farmers displaced, from Friends of the Earth Nigeria, is left out: EJAtlas quotes the same group elsewhere as saying 60,000 people 'risk' impacts. The company denies taking customary land and disputes the village-burning report.

lvwhy.land: A Socfin-controlled plantation expanded into forest reserves and farmland under military guard.
lvwhy.priv: The plantation passed from the federal government to Socfin in the 1990s privatization wave (Mongabay).

cases.title: Sino-Metals Leach Tailings Dam Collapse into the Kafue River
cases.place: Chambishi, Copperbelt Province, Zambia
cases.point: Sino-Metals Leach tailings dam area near Chambishi (EJAtlas coordinates, approximate)

lenders.name: China Nonferrous Mining (CNMC) (China), through Sino-Metals Leach Zambia (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Sino-Metals Leach owns the tailings dam; its holding company CNMC records its 5,754 tonnes of copper cathode in 2024 (EWN/AFP). The mine is owned by a Chinese state-owned enterprise (Wikipedia). NFC Africa Mining owns the land the dam stood on (EWN/AFP).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. Chambishi lies in an economic and trade cooperation zone that Zambia agreed with China in 2007 (EJAtlas).

companies.name: Sino-Metals Leach Zambia
companies.role: Owner of the failed tailings dam

companies.name: NFC Africa Mining
companies.role: Owner of the surface land under the dam; co-defendant

cases.community: On 18 February 2025 the dam wall burst and acidic waste flowed into the Mwambashi River and on into the Kafue, which serves about 60% of Zambia's people (Wikipedia). The company put the spill at about 50 million litres; Drizit, the clean-up firm hired through a government tender, said it was about 20 times larger (EWN/AFP). Authorities shut off water to Kitwe, a city of about 700,000; groundnut and maize fields were destroyed; and on 23 February the fisheries ministry told residents not to eat fish from the Kafue basin (Wikipedia). Drizit found dangerous levels of cyanide, arsenic, copper, zinc, lead, chromium and cadmium (EWN/AFP). Farmers reported abdominal pain, skin irritation, vomiting and blood in urine, and said livestock died (EWN/AFP).
cases.ecosystem: Mass fish deaths and loss of birdlife were seen at least 100 km downstream; the air force dropped several hundred tonnes of lime into the river (Wikipedia).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported from the spill.
cases.outcome: The government suspended the mine and said the company would pay for all clean-up; its chairman apologised (Wikipedia). Drizit said Sino-Metals ended its contract a day before its final report was due (EWN/AFP). On 6 August 2025 the US Embassy ordered its staff out of the affected areas (Wikipedia). In September 2025, 176 residents sued Sino-Metals Leach and NFC Africa Mining, asking for $80 billion in escrow for remediation and compensation (EWN/AFP).

sources.title: Zambian farmers sue Chinese mining firms over toxic spill
2025 Sino-Metals Leach Zambia dam disaster
Sino Metals tailings dam failure in Chambishi, Zambia

cases.confidence_note: The spill volume is disputed (company 50 million litres; Drizit about 20 times more). Health complaints are as reported by the plaintiffs.

lvwhy.project: A Chinese state-owned copper firm's tailings dam failed and poisoned Zambia's main river.

cases.title: Shell's Bonga Offshore Spill of December 2011
cases.place: Bonga field (OML 118), offshore Niger Delta, Nigeria
cases.point: Odioma, Brass, Bayelsa State, one of the coastal communities the slick reached (EJAtlas); the Bonga field itself is about 120 km offshore

lenders.name: Shell (United Kingdom/Netherlands), through SNEPCo (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Shell's subsidiary SNEPCo operates the Bonga field and holds 55% of the licence; ExxonMobil holds 20% (EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. Bonga was producing about 200,000 barrels a day at the time (Reuters).

companies.name: Shell Nigeria Exploration and Production Company (SNEPCo)

cases.community: On 20 December 2011 about 40,000 barrels of crude leaked while a tanker was loading at the Shell-operated platform, according to Nigeria's spill agency NOSDRA; the slick covered about 950 square km and hurt fishing livelihoods (Reuters). Communities in Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa and Delta states were affected; NOSDRA put the affected communities at over 350 (ThisDay; AllAfrica). Protesters in Abuja in 2024 said the spill made fishing impossible, linked it to health problems, and said they had sought compensation since 2012 without result (AllAfrica).
cases.ecosystem: Oil spread over about 950 square km of sea and coast (Reuters).
cases.outcome: NOSDRA set $1.8 billion for damage and lost income plus $1.8 billion in punitive damages (ThisDay). In November 2014 the National Assembly said Shell should pay $3.96 billion; the resolution was non-binding (Reuters). On 24 May 2018 the Federal High Court in Lagos dismissed SNEPCo's challenge to NOSDRA's power to fine it (ThisDay; AllAfrica). Shell said it accepted responsibility for the spill and had cleaned the area (Reuters). An EFCC source told Premium Times that the UK Supreme Court ruled in Shell's favour in 2023, with the communities' main claim still pending in the UK (AllAfrica).

sources.title: Nigeria's parliament says Shell should pay $4 billion for 2011 oil spill
NOSDRA to Shell: Obey court order, pay $3.6bn fine over Bonga oil spill
Nigeria: Bonga oil spill victims protest at Ministry of Justice (Premium Times)
Shell Bonga Oil Spill, Nigeria

cases.confidence_note: Proposed fines have ranged from $3.6 billion to $11.5 billion across agencies, and the fine had not been paid by 2024. The account of the UK ruling comes from an unnamed EFCC official.

lvwhy.project: An offshore field run by Shell's subsidiary spilled about 40,000 barrels onto fishing coasts.

cases.title: TVI Pacific's Canatuan Mine on Subanon Sacred Land
cases.place: Mount Canatuan, Siocon, Zamboanga del Norte, Philippines
cases.point: Mount Canatuan mine site (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.name: TVI Pacific (Canada), through TVI Resource Development Philippines (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Its Philippine subsidiary received the mining agreement on 23 October 1996 and mined gold, silver, copper and zinc from 2004 to 2014; EJAtlas calls it the first mine run by a foreign company under the 1995 Mining Act (EJAtlas; MiningWatch Canada).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. TVI claimed possible World Bank IFC financing, for which MiningWatch found no evidence (MiningWatch Canada).
cases.community: TVI deployed more than 100 armed guards in the mid-1990s and imposed checkpoints and an economic blockade on the community that lasted eight years by 2003; several people were shot and wounded trying to bring goods in (MiningWatch Canada). In May-June 2003 the paramilitary SCAA unit guarding the mine seized fuel, destroyed small-scale miners' ball and rod mills, fired near residents and demolished a miner's mill house (MiningWatch Canada). The mine bulldozed the tip of Mount Canatuan, the Subanon's most sacred site, inside land covered by their 2003 ancestral title of 8,213 hectares (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: Reported tailings releases into waterways and declining fish stocks (EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: An SCAA paramilitary unit, armed and trained by the army and paid by companies, guarded the mine; 88 recruits were trained in April-May 2003 (MiningWatch Canada). In 1999 police and guards beat picketers and arrested Subanon leader Onsino Mato (MiningWatch Canada).
cases.killed_note: Not counted: on 19 May 2003 seven masked men kidnapped Parcilito Tambuko, whose leader wore army-style overalls; he was killed and soldiers of the local battalion removed his body the next day, and the killers were not identified (MiningWatch Canada). An ambush on a TVI truck on 26 December 2002 killed 13 people, mostly local company workers, by unidentified armed assailants (MiningWatch Canada).
cases.outcome: The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination took up the Subanon of Mount Canatuan under its early-warning procedure in 2007 and in 2008 and 2010 cited mining by transnational companies without prior consent (UN CERD). In May 2011 TVI admitted fault in an indigenous justice trial and agreed to pay fines; mining ended in 2014 when ore ran out (EJAtlas).

CERD early warning decisions on the Philippines (CERD/C/62/18; A/63/18; A/65/18)
sources.publisher: UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (via Bayefsky.com)

sources.title: Mt. Canatuan Gold Mine on Subanon Ancestral Lands, Philippines

cases.confidence_note: The incident list comes from community members and observers reported by MiningWatch Canada; the UN committee's concern is on record but it did not rule on specific incidents. Area violence also involved MILF rebels and the army.

lvwhy.project: A Canadian company's open-pit mine was guarded by an army-trained paramilitary unit.

cases.title: Plantations du Haut Penja and the Jailing of Mayor Paul Eric Kingué
cases.place: Njombé-Penja, Moungo, Littoral Region, Cameroon
cases.point: Njombé-Penja (EJAtlas coordinates, approximate)

lenders.name: Compagnie Fruitière (France), through Plantations du Haut Penja (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Owner of PHP, the banana producer in Njombé-Penja (Transparency International). For ten years PHP and two other foreign-owned firms shared about five million euros a year in EU banana subsidies (Libération, via EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded for the plantations themselves; Libération reported EU banana-sector support to PHP (via EJAtlas).
cases.community: In 2007 Njombé-Penja's mayor, Paul Eric Kingué, accused PHP of not paying tax on its operations. After protests in the town he was arrested in February 2008 and charged with organising them, and was held in Nkongsamba and Douala prisons for about seven years (Transparency International). Libération reported he was accused of taking part in vandalism against PHP and sentenced to six years (via EJAtlas). Transparency International also reports allegations that PHP used pesticides banned in Europe, harming workers and land. Residents told Libération their only river was polluted, and a health official said respiratory and skin diseases were the most common after malaria (via EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: Kingué was arrested in February 2008 and jailed until 16 July 2015. In August 2014 the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his detention arbitrary and called for his release and compensation (Transparency International).
cases.killed_note: No deaths tied to the company are reported.
cases.outcome: The prosecutor dropped the charges in early 2015, and the Supreme Court in Yaoundé ordered Kingué's release on 16 July 2015 (Transparency International). PHP denies all the allegations, and says it has paid its taxes; an open letter signed by more than 5,000 of its roughly 6,000 workers said it pays well and provides medical care (Transparency International).

sources.title: Cameroonian corruption fighter Paul Eric Kingue is free
Slippery justice: the travails of a whistleblower in Cameroon
Plantation de Haut Penja, Cameroon

cases.confidence_note: The detention and the UN finding are documented. That it was retaliation for accusing PHP is the view of Transparency International; PHP denies the tax and pesticide allegations. Pollution and health claims come from residents quoted by Libération.

lvwhy.project: A mayor who accused a French-owned banana company of tax fraud spent seven years in jail on charges later dropped.

cases.title: SOCO's Oil Exploration in Virunga National Park and Attacks on Its Critics
cases.place: Virunga National Park (Block V), North Kivu, DR Congo
cases.point: Plains south of Lake Edward inside Virunga National Park, within the Block V area (approximate)

lenders.name: SOCO International (United Kingdom) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Signed a production-sharing agreement with the DRC government in 2006 and received its exploration permit for Block V, more than half of it inside the park, in October 2011 (EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The exploration was an oil licence granted by the Congolese state inside a UNESCO World Heritage site (EJAtlas).

companies.name: SOCO International plc
companies.role: Operator of the Block V exploration

cases.community: In September 2013 the park's central sector chief was warned he would be killed if he kept opposing SOCO's work; days later military and intelligence officers beat, arrested and detained him. On 15 April 2014 park director Emmanuel de Mérode was shot and seriously wounded by three armed men in military uniform, and in the following week activists received threats such as 'You are going to die for nothing like de Mérode' (Human Rights Watch). On 31 January 2014 a 300-person march against SOCO organised by a farmers' cooperative in Rutshuru was met by police, and some protesters were detained and beaten, according to local press cited by EJAtlas.
cases.suppression: Human Rights Watch documented arbitrary arrests by authorities and attacks by unidentified assailants on rangers and activists who criticised the exploration, and said Congolese military and intelligence officials implicated in many cases allegedly received money from SOCO (Human Rights Watch).
cases.killed_note: No deaths are tied to the exploration in these sources; de Mérode survived his wounds.
cases.outcome: WWF complained to the UK OECD National Contact Point in October 2013; after mediation, SOCO agreed on 11 June 2014 to halt exploration in Virunga and not to explore in any other World Heritage site (SOMO). SOCO condemned the attack on de Mérode, denied any role in threats, violence or bribery, and said it would look into the bribery allegations (Human Rights Watch).

sources.title: Dispatches: Congo's Virunga park rangers, activists still need justice
SOCO to halt its oil exploration activities in Virunga
Oil drilling in Virunga National Park by SOCO International plc, DR of Congo

cases.confidence_note: The attacks and arrests are documented by Human Rights Watch, but the payments to officers are allegations; SOCO denies any role. Who shot de Mérode has not been established.

lvwhy.project: A UK company's oil exploration in a World Heritage park was followed by arrests, beatings and threats against rangers and activists who opposed it.

cases.title: Senhuile's 20,000-Hectare Lease in the Ndiaël Reserve
cases.place: Ndiaël reserve, Saint-Louis Region, Senegal
cases.point: Ndiaël reserve area (EJAtlas coordinates, approximate)

lenders.name: Tampieri Financial Group (Italy) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Holds 51% of Senhuile SA; Senéthanol, 75% owned by ABE Italia, holds the other 49% (Oakland Institute; La Repubblica).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. Presidential decrees of 20 March 2012 removed protection from 26,550 ha of the reserve and leased 20,000 ha to the company for 50 years; a new president repealed them in April 2012 and reinstated them on 6 August 2012 (Oakland Institute).
cases.community: About 9,000 people, mainly semi-nomadic herders, live in the project area; residents say 40 villages rely on the land, which grazed about 40,000 cows, 20,000 sheep and 21,000 goats and was the region's only remaining pasture (Oakland Institute). Residents say the project cut their cattle off from grazing and water (La Repubblica). In June 2013 three children drowned after falling into the project's open canals (Oakland Institute). The report also records allegations that the company destroyed sacred sites, cemeteries and schools (Oakland Institute).
cases.ecosystem: Land in a former wildlife reserve was cleared for irrigated crops; an impact study was finished in November 2012, months after clearing began (Oakland Institute).
cases.suppression: Residents report verbal intimidation and physical assaults by police deployed to block access to the project (Oakland Institute). During the 2011 clashes at the earlier Fanaye site, six residents were arrested and held for ten days (Oakland Institute).
cases.killed_note: Not counted: on 26 October 2011 at Fanaye, where the project was first planned, clashes between supporters and opponents led to two deaths and many wounded (Oakland Institute; La Repubblica); the sources do not say who killed them. Three children who drowned in the project's open canals in June 2013 are not counted as violent deaths (Oakland Institute).
cases.outcome: An ActionAid and Re:Common petition asking Tampieri to withdraw gathered over 24,000 signatures in a week (La Repubblica). Chief executive Giovanni Tampieri said the company works 'in the interests of local people', uses no pesticides and leaves areas open to residents, and denied land grabbing (La Repubblica).

cases.title: Michelin's Tyre Plant on Thervoy Village's Common Forest
cases.place: Thervoy Kandigai, Tiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu, India
cases.point: Thervoy Kandigai SIPCOT industrial park (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.name: Michelin (France) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: In November 2009 Michelin acquired land near Thervoy from the Tamil Nadu government and began building what the complaint called India's largest tyre factory (OECD Watch).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The state industrial agency SIPCOT acquired 1,127 acres of village common land for the zone (EJAtlas).
cases.community: The complaint to the French OECD contact point says about 450 hectares of collective forest used for farming and grazing was destroyed, depriving villagers of their main livelihood, and that eighteen other villages were affected by linked infrastructure. Villagers, mainly a Dalit community living there for over two hundred years, and a nearby Irula indigenous community say they were not consulted (OECD Watch). EJAtlas reports that trees were cut and the area fenced, the channel of a stream feeding the grazing land was blocked, reducing its flow, and a lake was filled with excavated soil.
cases.ecosystem: About 450 ha of common forest cleared (complainants, via OECD Watch); a stream channel blocked and a lake filled (EJAtlas).

cases.title: MIDROC's Lega Dembi Gold Mine and the 2018 Shakiso Protests

cases.point: Lega Dembi mine (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.role: MIDROC Gold took over the state mine in 1997; EJAtlas reports it paid $172 million in the privatization (The New Humanitarian; VOA; EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The state-run mine was sold to MIDROC Gold in 1997, and its licence was renewed for ten years in 2018 (The New Humanitarian; VOA).

companies.name: MIDROC group (Mohammed Hussein al-Amoudi)
companies.role: Parent group, owned by Ethiopian-born Saudi billionaire Mohammed Hussein al-Amoudi

cases.community: A March 2018 environmental audit by Addis Ababa University's business enterprise found cyanide 'in considerable amounts' in water and soil outside the tailings dam; three tailings ponds had no liners or fences and two were used for drinking water without warnings (The New Humanitarian). An unreleased 2018 survey by the Ethiopian Public Health Institute of nearly 3,000 households found 384 people with chronic illness or disability, and the Shakiso area has the highest birth-defect rate measured in Ethiopia (The New Humanitarian). cases.title: Philex's Padcal Tailings Spill of August 2012

cases.title: MRC's Tormin Beach Mine and the West Coast Cliff Collapses
cases.place: Tormin mine, near Lutzville, Matzikama, Western Cape, South Africa
cases.point: Tormin mine processing plant on the coast (EJAtlas coordinates)

lenders.name: Mineral Commodities Ltd (MRC) (Australia), through Mineral Sands Resources (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Australian owner of the Tormin mineral sands mine, which began operating in November 2013 (EJAtlas; GroundUp gives March 2014).

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. In 2015, its first full year, Tormin reported a $12.9 million profit on $48 million turnover (GroundUp).
cases.community: The sea cliff in front of the processing plant began collapsing around February 2015, with seepage from the mine visible; mining was reported inside the 10-metre buffer at the foot of the cliffs (GroundUp). Satellite images from March 2018 showed four more collapses, most as large as or larger than the 2015 one (GroundUp, via Daily Maverick). An independent audit found unlawful clearing of a further 3.9 hectares and an unauthorised 2.2-hectare dam (Daily Maverick). lenders.name: ExxonMobil (United States), through Mobil Producing Nigeria (foreign investor)

lenders.name: Dharni Sampda (India), through Bondoukou Manganèse S.A. (foreign investor)

cases.conditions: No lender is recorded. The mining permit expired in 2019 and was renewed without consulting the community (Advocates for Community Alternatives).
cases.community: Residents say tailings contaminated the creeks, leaving families to drink from the river, and report breathing problems and stomach illness; a plaintiff said the doctor who treated his six-year-old son told him the boy died of a stomach illness from drinking the river water (Advocates for Community Alternatives). Blasting cracked house walls, and farmland and cashew and fruit trees were lost (Advocates for Community Alternatives). The state told the ECOWAS Court that reports by its anti-pollution centre and environment agency led to an order of 11 November 2015 suspending the company; it resumed in 2016 with corrective measures (Modern Ghana).
cases.ecosystem: Tailings in creeks and dust in the air; a study sponsored by a local group found poor air quality (Advocates for Community Alternatives).
cases.killed_note: A plaintiff said a doctor linked his six-year-old son's death to contaminated river water (Advocates for Community Alternatives); not counted as a violent death.
cases.outcome: In a judgment reported by the Ghana News Agency in January 2024, the ECOWAS Court of Justice found Côte d'Ivoire liable for violating the rights of the Similimi village head and nine other residents to a healthy environment and health, private and family life, an adequate standard of living and food, freedom of religion and minority culture; it rejected the property-rights claim and collective compensation, ordered 50 million CFA francs for each of the ten applicants, resettlement of Similimi residents, rapid environmental restoration and accountability for those responsible (GNA; Modern Ghana).
